title: When it comes to AI in education, who’s the adult in the room?
author: Michelle Brown
summary: Michelle Brown argues that education has entered analysis paralysis over AI, producing frameworks, task forces and white papers while tools enter classrooms faster than anyone can evaluate them. She notes that Common Sense Media paused its learning-potential ratings to focus on AI risk, that 37 states have published AI guidance, and that thirty-seven frameworks are not a shared instructional point of view. Her central claim is that schools and teachers are being asked to solve a governance problem without a pedagogical architecture grounded in knowledge-building and evidence. She praises New York City's one-year ban on student-facing generative AI as an honest acknowledgment that no such perspective exists yet. She calls for clear subject-specific principles, simple classroom standards, evidence requirements before tools enter schools, quick evaluation mechanisms and someone accountable for coordination.
points: Frameworks that are broad enough to fit anything cannot tell a district which tools to approve or a teacher whether to allow a chatbot for brainstorming.
Common Sense Media's shift from asking whether a tool helps kids learn to asking whether it will hurt them signals a gap in quality evaluation.
Individual teachers cannot be expected to solve a system-level governance problem alongside teaching thirty children.
She asks for an instructional center of gravity: subject-specific principles, evidence filters for new tools and one accountable coordinator.
quotes: Having 37 frameworks is not a systems-level instructional architecture. Thirty-seven frameworks is not the same thing as a shared instructional point of view.
It’s shifted from asking “Does this help kids learn?” to “Will this hurt them?
We can’t–and shouldn’t–ask every teacher to independently solve a governance problem that belongs to the adults designing the system.
The problem with a broad enough framework is that almost anything can fit inside it.

But none of those statements tells a district which tools to approve or how to spot marketing edu-speak that overpromises. They don’t tell a teacher whether a student should use a chatbot to brainstorm an essay.
We need to establish a point of view, make a decision, measure the results and change course when the evidence changes.
Professional judgment matters. But professional judgment cannot substitute for system-level leadership.
We’re improvising. And our kids are absorbing the consequences. And they’re only in school once.
